stem: Checking finished products against a standard to find faults is an example of

options.rationale: Correct: faults are found by inspection or testing.
Quality assurance prevents faults through the whole system.
Benchmarking compares performance with the best firm.
JIT is an approach to inventory, not quality.

explanation: Quality control means inspecting or testing to find faults.

stem: Comparing a firm's performance with that of the best firm in order to find ways to improve is called

options.rationale: Correct: the firm measures itself against the best.
TQM makes everyone responsible for quality.
Sampling checks a few items to estimate the quality of a batch.
Rationalisation means cutting capacity.

explanation: Benchmarking compares the firm with the best performer.

stem: How does **quality assurance** differ from quality control?

options.content: It checks only the finished product before it is sent out
options.rationale: That is feedback quality control.

options.content: It involves only the inspectors in the factory
options.rationale: Quality assurance involves all workers.

options.content: It aims to prevent faults, not find them afterwards
options.rationale: Correct: prevention built into the system.

options.content: It never involves any training for the workers
options.rationale: Training is a typical part of quality assurance.

explanation: Quality assurance prevents faults through standards and organisation; control detects them.

stem: Which of these is a **feed-forward** quality control?

options.content: Inspecting finished goods before they are sent to customers
options.rationale: That is feedback control.

options.content: Testing materials before they are used in production
options.rationale: Correct: inputs are checked before work starts.
That is feedback control.

options.content: Checking items as they move along the production line
options.rationale: That is concurrent control.

explanation: Feed-forward control checks inputs and plans before production begins.

stem: A fictional furniture maker lets a small group of workers meet each week to suggest how to cut mistakes in finishing. This is an example of

options.rationale: Benchmarking compares with the best firm outside the group.
Correct: a small group solving quality problems.
Inspection is checking items, not group problem-solving.
No work is moved abroad.

explanation: A small group of workers meeting to solve problems is a quality circle (kaizen group).
hints: The workers meet regularly to solve problems.

stem: Why is random sampling used instead of inspecting every item when the test destroys the product?

options.content: Sampling is always more accurate than checking every item
options.rationale: Checking every item would be more accurate if it were possible.

options.content: Customers prefer products that have been tested
options.rationale: Testing every item is not possible in this case.

options.content: Inspecting every item would leave nothing to sell
options.rationale: Correct: destructive tests can only be applied to a sample.

options.content: Sampling removes the need for any standards
options.rationale: Standards are needed to judge the sample.

explanation: With destructive testing, only a sample can be tested.
hints: Think about what happens to an item that has been destroyed by testing.

stem: Which conclusion is the **best-supported judgement** on whether a small firm should introduce TQM?

options.content: Yes, because TQM guarantees that no faults will ever occur
options.rationale: No system can guarantee zero faults.

options.content: No, because quality has no effect on the sales of a firm
options.rationale: Quality affects reputation and sales.

options.content: Yes, because TQM costs nothing to introduce or to run
options.rationale: Training and time have a cost.

options.content: It depends on whether staff are committed and the savings exceed the cost
options.rationale: Correct: success depends on staff and on cost-benefit.

explanation: A strong judgement names the conditions: committed staff and net benefit.
hints: TQM needs the cooperation of workers and costs time and money.

stem: Quality control focuses on finding faults, whereas quality assurance focuses on preventing them.
explanation: True. Quality control detects faults by inspection or testing; quality assurance organises the whole process so that faults do not occur.

stem: A high-quality product must always be expensive.
explanation: False. Quality means meeting customers' expectations and being fit for purpose. A low-priced product can be of high quality for its price.
hints: Quality is judged against what the customer expects at that price.

stem: Match each term to its description.

right.content: Making every employee responsible for quality
Comparing performance with the best firm
Inspecting or testing to find faults
Preventing faults by organising the whole system

explanation: Each term has a distinct meaning in quality management.

stem: Choose the correct word for each gap.

payload.template: A small group of workers that meets regularly to solve quality problems is called a quality {{blank:a}}, and the Japanese word for continuous improvement is {{blank:b}}.

explanation: Quality circles are small problem-solving groups; kaizen means continuous improvement.

stem: State **one** benefit to a business of high quality.
explanation: Loyalty, higher prices, fewer returns and waste, and a good reputation are benefits of quality.

stem: An inspector checks a random sample of 150 items from a fictional factory and finds 6 faulty. Calculate the defect rate in the sample as a percentage to one decimal place.
explanation: Defect rate = 6 ÷ 150 × 100 = 4.0%. Dividing by the good items (144) gives 4.2%.
workedSolution: 1. Defect rate = 6 ÷ 150 × 100 = 4.0%. Dividing by the good items (144) gives 4.2%.

stem: Sampling suggests that 2.5% of the items in a fictional batch of 8,000 are faulty. How many faulty items would you expect in the whole batch?
explanation: Expected faulty items = 2.5% × 8,000 = 200. Dividing 8,000 by 2.5 gives 3,200.
workedSolution: 1. Expected faulty items = 2.5% × 8,000 = 200. Dividing 8,000 by 2.5 gives 3,200.

stem: A fictional tile maker produces 4,800 tiles a month, of which 2.5% are defective. Each defective tile costs US\$6.50 in scrap and lost materials. Calculate the monthly cost of defects.
explanation: 120 defective tiles at US\$6.50 each cost US\$780. Multiplying all the tiles by the unit cost gives US\$31,200, which is the cost of all tiles.
workedSolution:
1. Defective tiles = 2.5% × 4,800 = 120.
2. Cost = 120 × US\$6.50 = US\$780 a month.
hints: Find the number of defective tiles first.

stem: A fictional bakery's total yearly quality costs (prevention, inspection and failure) fell from US\$52,000 to US\$41,600 after it introduced quality assurance. Calculate the percentage change in total quality cost to one decimal place. Give a fall as a negative number.
hints: Divide the change in cost by the cost before the change.

stem: Explain **one** reason why quality is important to a business.

points.description: Good quality keeps customers satisfied, so they buy again and recommend the product
Poor quality causes returns, waste and a damaged reputation, which raise costs

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Good quality keeps customers satisfied, so they buy again and recommend the product. Poor quality causes returns and waste and damages the reputation, which raises costs.

explanation: One mark for the effect on customers and one for the effect on cost.

stem: Rudo owns a fictional clothing factory in Gweru that has many returned shirts with loose buttons. Explain **two** ways she could improve quality.

points.description: Train the machinists in how to attach buttons correctly
Application: trained workers make fewer faulty seams and buttons, so returns fall
Inspect shirts at each stage (concurrent control) before they are packed
Application: loose buttons would be found and repaired before delivery to customers

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Rudo could train the machinists to attach buttons correctly, so there are fewer faulty shirts and fewer returns. She could also inspect shirts at each stage before they are packed, so loose buttons are found and repaired before delivery to customers.

explanation: Two methods, each developed for the factory.
hints: Think about prevention and about inspection.

stem: Analyse how a quality circle may improve both quality and morale.

points.description: Workers who do the job know where faults arise and can suggest practical solutions
Solutions based on their ideas reduce faults and waste
Being asked for ideas gives workers a sense of involvement and recognition
Higher motivation leads to more care and fewer errors

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Workers who do the job know where faults arise and can suggest practical solutions, which reduce faults and waste. Being asked for ideas gives them a sense of involvement and recognition, so their motivation rises and they take more care.

explanation: A chain from worker ideas to fewer faults and higher motivation.
hints: Think about knowledge and about involvement.

stem: A fictional bottling company wants to benchmark its delivery times against the best firm in its industry. Assess the usefulness of benchmarking.

points.description: It shows how far the firm is behind the best and sets targets
It identifies methods that could be copied
It needs information from rivals, which may be hard to get
Methods that suit another firm may not suit this one
Judgement with a condition, for example: useful if the firm can adapt the best practice to its own situation

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Benchmarking shows how far the firm is behind the best and sets targets, and it can identify methods to copy. But information from rivals may be hard to get, and methods that suit another firm may not suit this one. It is useful if the company can adapt the best practice to its own situation.

explanation: Both sides, then a conditional judgement.
hints: Weigh the targets and ideas against the difficulty of getting information.

stem:
A fictional bakery in Masvingo moved from relying on inspection towards quality assurance. Its yearly quality costs before and after the change are shown.

| Quality cost (US\$ a year) | Before | After |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| Prevention (training, maintenance) | 4,000 | 9,500 |
| Inspection and testing | 7,500 | 4,000 |
| Failure (rework, returns, scrap) | 23,500 | 9,000 |

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Calculate the total quality cost after the change.
parts.explanation: 9,500 + 4,000 + 9,000 = US\$22,500. Before the change the total was US\$35,000.
parts.workedSolution: 1. 9,500 + 4,000 + 9,000 = US\$22,500. Before the change the total was US\$35,000.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Into which type of quality cost does the training of bakers fall?

options.rationale: Inspection means checking for faults.
Failure costs arise from faults that have occurred.
Benchmarking is not a cost category in the table.
Correct: training prevents faults from occurring.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Explain why spending more on prevention reduced the bakery's total quality cost.

points.description: Prevention spending rose from US\$4,000 to US\$9,500
Fewer faults occurred, so failure costs fell from US\$23,500 to US\$9,000
The fall in failure and inspection costs was greater than the rise in prevention

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Prevention spending rose from US\$4,000 to US\$9,500, but fewer faults occurred, so failure costs fell from US\$23,500 to US\$9,000 and inspection costs also fell. The saving on failure and inspection was greater than the extra spent on prevention.

parts.explanation: Prevention up, failure down, net fall.
hints: Compare the change in each line.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: Assess whether the bakery should now stop inspecting its bread altogether.

points.description: Inspection costs US\$4,000, which could be saved
Without inspection, faults that still occur would reach customers
Judgement with a condition, for example: keep a small sample inspection because failure costs of US\$9,000 remain

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Stopping inspection would save US\$4,000, but faults that still occur would reach customers and harm the bakery's reputation. Failure costs of US\$9,000 remain, so a small sample inspection should be kept until defects are lower.

parts.explanation: Saving, risk and a conditional judgement.
hints: Remember that some faults still occur.

explanation: Total quality cost fell from US\$35,000 to US\$22,500. Prevention reduced failure costs by more than it cost.
hints: Add the three lines for each year.

stem: Zambezi Tiles is a fictional tile maker in Bulawayo. It makes 50,000 tiles a year and 6% are defective, each costing US\$2.80 in scrap. The owner is considering total quality management (TQM), with training, quality circles and a new system of checks at each stage. The programme would cost US\$6,500 in the first year and US\$2,000 a year afterwards, and is expected to cut the defect rate to 2%. Customers have complained about late deliveries caused by remaking faulty tiles. Some supervisors say that quality circles will waste time.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Calculate the yearly cost of defective tiles at present.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Analyse **one** way in which TQM could benefit Zambezi Tiles besides lower scrap costs.

points.description: Fewer defective tiles means fewer tiles to remake, so deliveries are quicker
Application: customers have complained about late deliveries caused by remaking
Better delivery and quality improve the firm's reputation
A better reputation could win repeat orders and allow higher prices

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: With fewer defective tiles there are fewer to remake, so deliveries are quicker and the complaints about late delivery should fall. A better reputation for quality and delivery could bring repeat orders and allow the firm to charge higher prices.

parts.explanation: A chain from fewer defects to delivery and reputation.
hints: Use the complaints about late deliveries.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Evaluate whether Zambezi Tiles should introduce TQM.

points.description: Defects fall from 3,000 to 1,000 tiles, saving 2,000 × US\$2.80 = US\$5,600 a year
In year 1 the net result is a loss of US\$900 (5,600 − 6,500)
From year 2 the net gain is US\$3,600 a year (5,600 − 2,000)
Better delivery and reputation are further benefits that the figures do not show
Supervisors' doubts and the time taken by quality circles are risks
The expected 2% defect rate is an estimate and may not be achieved
Judgement with a reason, for example: yes, because the programme pays from year 2
Condition or time-frame, for example: if the supervisors support it and results are reviewed after a year

levels.descriptor: General points on TQM with little use of the figures.
Reasons for and against using the figures in the case.
Balanced evaluation using the yearly gains, with a justified judgement and a condition.

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Cutting defects from 6% to 2% saves 2,000 tiles a year, worth US\$5,600. In the first year the programme costs US\$6,500, so there is a loss of US\$900, but from the second year the net gain is US\$3,600 a year. Better delivery and reputation add further benefits. Against this, the 2% target is only an estimate, and supervisors doubt the value of quality circles. Zambezi Tiles should introduce TQM, because the gain from year 2 is clear, provided the supervisors are won over with training and results are reviewed after the first year.

parts.explanation: Saving US\$5,600 a year; net −US\$900 in year 1 and +US\$3,600 afterwards.
hints: Compare the saving with the cost in year 1 and in later years.

explanation: Defects cost US\$8,400 now. TQM saves US\$5,600 a year, so it pays from the second year; the judgement depends on staff support and the defect target.
hints: Defective tiles = defect rate × tiles made.
